messages.body_plain:
Hi Dylan,

I think those two issues are unrelated. For the chisq and AIC = NA that should also come with a message that those are printing as NA because you are estimating a fully saturated model (i.e., degrees of freedom = 0), as will be the case when you estimate a common factor with three indicators. Not something to be concerned about, you just can't model fit estimates in this case because the model is going to exactly fit the data.

The system is computationally singular error in the context of the common factor gwas will sometimes print with a reciprocal condition number. Is that number included in the error message?

-Andrew

Are the two (chisq=NA and the error) related?

> Dylan

> On Wednesday, July 29, 2020 at 10:51:28 AM UTC-4, Michel Nivard wrote:
> > So model fits the data well (briefly: the chisq test, which tests the model against a freely estimated covariance matrix isnt significant, which means the model doest describe the covariance significantly worse, CFI is 1, CFI ranges form 0 to 1 and is a comparison against an "empty" model where the traits are uncorrelated, 1 means good ft compared to an empty model. then the SRMR quantifies the (weighted I believe) squared difference between the observed and expected covariance matrix, its lowish here, which is good.
> >
> > This all being said, the model fits the covariance matrix well, but the factor doest explain a lot of the heritable variation in for example TS ( .114^2 / (.114^2 + .199) = ~6%)
> >
> > so if you added TS because you are interested in genetic effects on TS be forewarned this factor isn't really a reflection of TS (because TS doest correlate to highly with the other traits I think)
> >
> > Your model is slower than usual I'd sya, but not entirely unheard off. To speed things up you can specify starting values near (but not at!) the final estimates and perhaps things go a bit quicker.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Moreh,

I would recommend against using the word "causal" unless you are referring to something like Mendelian Randomization. I take it that you are referring to whether you can specify a model that includes paths from the SNP to all GWAS phenotypes. That is straightforward to do using the standard lavaan syntax. Keep in mind that you typically can't have a model that estimates paths from the SNPs to all indicators of a factor and additionally estimates paths to the factor. Such a model is typically underidentified.

Also note that the Q statistic for the common factor GWAS compares a model with a path from the SNP to the factor to a model with paths from the SNP to all indicators (but not the factor). This is described in the original Grotzinger at all paper in Nature Human Behaviour, and further discussed in the supplement to the forthcoming de la Fuente paper (see section "Interpreting the Heterogeneity Statistic" and Figure S9). Papers below:

de la Fuente, J., Davies, J., Grotzinger, A. D., Tucker-Drob, E. M., & Deary. (in press). A general dimension of genetic sharing across diverse cognitive traits inferred from molecular data. Dear Genomic SEM Team,

I am restricted to use an R version < 4.0.0, though the newest GenomicSEM / lavaan release "requires" the most recent "mnormt" package, which in turn requires R version >= 4.0.0. Due to this dependency the GenomicSEM / lavaan package cannot be installed. I guess a solution could be to install an older mnormt package, though I am not certain that this is compatible with the requirements of both the GenomicSEM as well as the lavaan packages.

Could you provide advice how to solve or circumvent this issue, and comment on potential dependencies between mnormt, lavaan and GenomicSEM versions?

Thank you,
Ulrich

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ravi,
Unless additional constraints are imposed, a common factor requires a minimum of 3 indicators for identification. A factor model with two indicators will have 1 factor variance, 2 factor loadings, and 2 residual variances. Standard identification constraints are to fix either a loading or the factor variance to 1.0. This leaves you with 4 free parameters. Your rG matrix however only has  3 pieces of information (1 genetic covariance and 2 genetic variances), so your model is under identified (df = -1). Additionally, the genetic correlation between your two variables is 1.0, which may lead to further issues.
I hope that helps.
Elliot

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ravi,

The correction for sample overlap in models without SNPs is not an extra option but intrinsic in the estimation method. The correction for sample overlap in models with SNPs takes advantage of the cross-trait intercepts from LDSC to populate the relevant portions of Vfull. This is automated when using the functions that we provide for including SNPs in the model, and does not require special options.

You can read about how sample overlap factors into LDSC by looking into the original LDSC publications by Bulik Sullivan et al., and by reading more recent expositions such as https://doi.org/10.1101/310565.

The off-diagonal elements of Vldsc are estimated in multivariable LDSC through the same jacknife resampling as conventional LDSC. Resampling empirically estimates the sampling distribution of parameter estimates, so it is straightforward to estimate these distributions together for multiple parameters and obtain estimates of their dependencies (samping covariances). Our source code is open so you can examine the details of how this works if you are so inclined.

I believe that the formula for the sandwich correction of the GenomicSEM estimates using V is provided in the Grotzinger et al paper, and can also be found in our open source code. A great paper on how these corrections is the 2014 Savalei paper that we cite: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2013.824793

Cheers,

Elliot
